The primary stand of the insurance company is that the person driving the vehicle did not have a

Chapter II contains Sections 3, 4 and 5 of the Act relating to licensing of drivers driving the motor

Where the claim relates to own damage claims, it cannot be adjudicated by the insurance company.
But it has to be decided by an other forum i.e. forum created under the Consumer Protection Act,
1985 (in short the 'CP Act'). Before the Tribunal, there were essentially three parties i.e. the insurer,
insured and the claimants. On the contrary, before the consumer forums there were two parties i.e.
owner of the vehicle and the insurer. The claimant does not come in to the picture. Therefore, these

args.question: What must an owner do to check a driver's licence before employing them, and does failing to check defeat the insurer's defence?

supporting.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
supporting.principle: The owner's duty is to check whether the driver produces a driving licence which on the face of it looks genuine, and to take a test of the driver's competence. The owner is NOT expected to make enquiries with RTOs across the country to verify whether the licence is valid.
supporting.fact_alignment: The owner remained ex parte and adduced no evidence of having checked the licence. The court still held the insurer liable to pay third parties with recovery rights, not that the owner's failure defeated the insurer's defence.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the clearest statement in the corpus of what the owner must do. It quotes Lehru (2003) 3 SCC 338 verbatim: 'When an owner is hiring a driver he will therefore have to check whether the driver has a driving licence. If the driver produces a driving licence which on the face of it looks genuine, the owner is not expected to find out whether the licence has in fact been issued by a competent authority or not.'
supporting.quote: When an owner is hiring a driver he will therefore have to check whether the driver has a driving licence. If the driver produces a driving licence which on the face of it looks genuine, the owner is not expected to find out whether the licence has in fact been issued by a competent authority or not. The owner would then take the test of the driver. If he finds that the driver is competent to drive the vehicle, he will hire the driver.

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: The insurer has a statutory liability to pay third-party compensation even if there is a breach of policy conditions (invalid driving licence), and is entitled to recover from the insured. The owner's failure to check does not defeat the insurer's defence entirely — it triggers pay-and-recover.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver was not competent to drive a transport/commercial vehicle. The court held the insurer liable to pay third parties with recovery rights.
supporting.why_it_matters: Establishes that even where breach is proved, the insurer's remedy is pay-and-recover, not complete absolution, in third-party claims. The owner's failure to check does not let the insurer off the hook to the third party.
supporting.quote: The insurer who is made statutorily liable to pay compensation to third parties on account of the certificate of insurance issued shall be entitled to recover from the insured the amount paid to the third parties, if there was any breach of policy conditions on account of the vehicle being driven without a valid driving licence.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
supporting.principle: Where the driver holds only an LMV licence without the specific authorisation/badge required to drive a transport vehicle, there is a breach of policy conditions. The insurer must pay the third party and recover from the insured owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had an LMV licence but no badge/authorisation to drive a tourist maxi cab (transport vehicle). The insurer proved the breach through the Motor Vehicles Inspector's evidence.
supporting.why_it_matters: Shows the insurer can discharge its burden of proving breach by examining the Motor Vehicles Inspector and adducing licence records. Once breach is proved, the remedy is pay-and-recover, not complete avoidance.
supporting.quote: The absence of any endorsement in the driving licence as to the issuance of authorisation to drive the transport vehicle and non-mention of allotment of badge number clearly shows that the 3rd Respondent was not in possession of a valid driving licence and that he was not duly licensed to drive the transport vehicle and there was violation of Policy conditions.

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Driving without a valid licence constitutes a fundamental and statutory breach of the insurance policy. However, to protect third-party rights, the insurer must pay first and recover from the owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: The owner allowed the driver to drive despite the driver having no driving licence at all. The owner did not produce the driver's licence despite being represented by counsel.
supporting.why_it_matters: Even in the most extreme case — no licence at all — the remedy is pay-and-recover, not complete absolution. The owner's failure to check does not defeat the insurer's defence; it triggers the pay-and-recover mechanism.
supporting.quote: When it is found that offending vehicle was driven by driver who was either holding no licence or a fake licence, then it amounts to violation of terms and conditions of policy and no liability can be fastened upon Insurance Company... But, on the said ground, the petitioner is third party, cannot be made to suffer due to fault of owner when the vehicle is covered with insurance at relevant point of time.

supporting.title: New India Assurance Co., Ltd., vs Yallavva W/O Yamanappa Dharnakeri
supporting.principle: Even if a breach of policy conditions under Section 149(2) is successfully proved, the insurer is bound to satisfy the third-party award and recover from the insured, unless fraud or collusion between the victim and the insured is established.
supporting.fact_alignment: Full Bench decision establishing that pay-and-recover applies to all breaches of policy conditions in third-party claims, regardless of whether the policy is statutory or contractual.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the strongest authority for the proposition that failing to check the licence does NOT defeat the insurer's defence — the insurer still gets pay-and-recover. The only exception is fraud/collusion between victim and insured.
supporting.quote: Even if there is any violation or breach of condition of a policy, the insurer has to discharge the initial burden of proving the grounds taken under Section 149(2) of the Act. In spite of that, the insurer has to indemnify the amount and can recover the same from the insured.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
supporting.principle: Where a special endorsement is required (e.g., for hazardous goods), the owner has a duty under Rule 132(5) of the Central Motor Vehicles Rules to ensure the driver holds the requisite endorsement. Failure constitutes breach entitling the insurer to pay-and-recover.
supporting.fact_alignment: The tanker driver had a valid licence for HGV/HTV but lacked the special endorsement for carrying hazardous goods. The court held the insurer liable to pay and recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Extends the owner's duty beyond just checking for a licence — the owner must also check that the driver has the specific endorsements required for the type of goods being carried. But even here, the remedy is pay-and-recover.
supporting.quote: As per Rule 132 (5) of Central Motor Vehicle Rule, 1989, it is the duty of the owner to ensure that the driver of the goods carriage carrying dangerous or hazardous goods holds a driving license as per the rule 9 of the aforesaid Central Motor Vehicles Rules.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd., vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar W/O Late ...
supporting.principle: When a driving licence is renewed more than 30 days after expiry, it takes effect only from the date of renewal and does not cover the interregnum. The owner who entrusts the vehicle during this period bears responsibility, but the insurer must still pay and recover.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver's licence expired on 30-04-2008, was renewed on 04-07-2008, and the accident occurred on 02-07-2008. The court held the driver did not hold a valid licence on the accident date.
supporting.why_it_matters: Even where the licence had lapsed and the owner entrusted the vehicle to a driver without a current licence, the remedy is pay-and-recover, not complete absolution of the insurer.
supporting.quote: Since it is the statutory right of the third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded either from the owner or the driver, as the vehicle in question is insured, the insurance company shall pay the amount and recover the same from driver or the insured.

adverse.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
adverse.principle: An insurer cannot avoid its statutory liability to pay compensation to third parties merely because the driver of a light motor vehicle did not have a specific endorsement on their licence to drive it as a commercial vehicle.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this to argue that the insurer cannot avoid liability at all — not even pay-and-recover — when the driver held a valid LMV licence but lacked a commercial endorsement. The Supreme Court held the insurer liable without granting recovery rights.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case turned on the specific finding that a Mahindra Maxi Cab is a light motor vehicle and the driver held a valid LMV licence. The Supreme Court held that no separate endorsement was needed to drive it as a commercial vehicle. This is distinguishable where: (a) the vehicle is a different class (e.g., heavy goods vehicle requiring a separate licence class), or (b) the driver had no licence at all, or (c) the licence was fake. The ratio is limited to the LMV/commercial endorsement overlap.
adverse.quote: Merely because the driver did not get any endorsement in the driving licence to drive Mahindra Maxi Cab, which is a light motor vehicle, the High Court has committed grave error of law in holding that the insurer is not liable to pay compensation because the driver was not holding the licence to drive the commercial vehicle.

adverse.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
adverse.principle: The mere non-renewal of an otherwise valid driving licence on the date of accident does not constitute a fundamental breach absolving the insurer of its third-party liability. The insurer is jointly and severally liable without recovery rights.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this to argue that an expired-but-subsequently-renewed licence is not a fundamental breach, and the insurer must pay without recovery rights. This directly undermines the insurer's defence that the owner failed to check licence currency.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case involved licences that had expired but were renewed shortly after the accident. The court emphasised that the drivers had held valid licences, were not disqualified, and the renewal showed they were always entitled to drive. Distinguishable where: (a) the licence was never renewed, (b) the gap between expiry and renewal exceeded 30 days (see doc_003, Parvathi Hebbar), or (c) the driver never held a valid licence for that class of vehicle at all.
adverse.quote: Mere fact that the driver of the offending vehicle had not got his driving licence renewed on the date of the accident and got it renewed subsequently would not amount to breach of condition of the policy as it cannot be said that there was violation of the condition of the exclusion clause.

adverse.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
adverse.principle: The Swaran Singh principles regarding third-party risks have no application to own-damage claims. A fake driving licence cannot be cured by subsequent renewal.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this to argue the opposite — that Swaran Singh DOES apply to third-party claims (which is the present context), and therefore the insurer must pay and recover. The case actually supports the insurer on the own-damage vs third-party distinction.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This judgment actually supports the insurer's position on the key point: it confirms that in third-party claims, the insurer must indemnify and recover from the insured. It only limits Swaran Singh for own-damage claims. The claimant will cite it for the proposition that a fake licence cannot be cured, but in third-party claims the insurer still has to pay and recover.
adverse.quote: The decision in Swaran Singh's case has no application to cases other than third party risks... In case of third party risks the insurer has to indemnify the amount and if so advised to recover the same from the insured.

adverse.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
adverse.principle: Driving without a valid licence is a fundamental and statutory breach. The insurer is not liable to indemnify the owner.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite the portion where the tribunal says 'the insurer is not liable to pay the compensation and he is absolved from its liability' to argue that the insurer should be completely absolved, leaving the claimant to recover only from the owner.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: Despite stating that the insurer is 'absolved from its liability', the tribunal ultimately ordered pay-and-recover to protect the third party. The claimant cannot extract the absolving language while ignoring the operative pay-and-recover order. The consistent line of authority (doc_025, doc_033, doc_027) confirms that third-party protection overrides the breach.
adverse.quote: It is held that the respondent No.2 is not liable to pay the compensation and he is absolved from its liability... But, on the said ground, the petitioner is third party, cannot be made to suffer due to fault of owner when the vehicle is covered with insurance at relevant point of time.

priority_arguments: 1. The owner's duty is limited: the owner need only check that the driver produces a licence that looks genuine on its face and take a test of driving competence. The owner is NOT required to verify with the RTO whether the licence is genuine (doc_027, quoting Lehru).

2. Even if the owner failed to check the licence entirely, the insurer's remedy in third-party claims is pay-and-recover, not complete absolution. The insurer must pay the claimant and then recover from the owner (doc_025, doc_033, doc_035, doc_024, doc_003).

3. The burden of proving breach is on the insurer. The insurer must prove not just that the driver lacked a valid licence, but that the owner was guilty of negligence or failed to exercise reasonable care (doc_027, doc_025, citing Swaran Singh).
4. Where the owner remained ex parte or adduced no evidence of having checked the licence, an adverse inference may be drawn, but the remedy remains pay-and-recover, not complete avoidance (doc_027).
5. The only exception where the insurer may be completely absolved is fraud or collusion between the victim and the insured (doc_025), which is extremely rare and fact-specific.
strategy.compensation_range: Not applicable — this is a liability/defence question, not a quantum question.
risks: 1. S.Iyyapan (doc_032) — Supreme Court held that missing commercial endorsement on an LMV licence does not let the insurer off the hook at all (no recovery rights). This is the most dangerous precedent for the insurer. Must be distinguished on vehicle class.

2. K.G. Srinivasamurthy (doc_034) — expired-but-renewed licence held not a fundamental breach; insurer liable without recovery. Must be distinguished where the licence gap exceeds 30 days or was never renewed.
3. The claimant may argue that the insurer must prove 'willful breach' by the owner — mere failure to check may not suffice if the licence looked genuine on its face (doc_027, doc_033).
4. If the insurer cannot prove the licence defect at all (e.g., no evidence from the RTO/MVI), the defence fails entirely and the insurer must pay without any recovery right.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: In third-party claims before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, the insurer should: (a) lead evidence from the Motor Vehicles Inspector/RTO to prove the licence defect; (b) examine the policy to show the relevant condition; (c) argue that breach is proved; but (d) concede that the third party must be paid, and seek a pay-and-recover order against the owner. Do NOT argue for complete absolution in third-party claims — the consistent line of authority rejects this. Reserve the argument for complete absolution only in own-damage claims (doc_031) or where fraud/collusion is proved.

caveats: This corpus does not contain the full text of Swaran Singh (2004) 3 SCC 297 or Lehru (2003) 3 SCC 338, which are the foundational Supreme Court authorities on this issue. The principles from those cases are cited and applied in multiple judgments within the corpus (doc_027, doc_033, doc_035, doc_025), so the corpus is consistent with them, but the original judgments are not directly available for verbatim citation.

The corpus contains no judgment where the insurer was completely absolved of liability (no pay-and-recover) solely because the owner failed to check the driver's licence. The consistent position across all relevant judgments is that the insurer must pay the third party and recover from the owner.

doc_002 (Liyakat Ali) and doc_028 (Sukumarbai) involve complete absolution of the insurer, but on entirely different grounds (non-agricultural use of tractor; passengers in private vehicle for hire) — not on licence verification. They are not relevant to this research question.

doc_031 (Laxmi Narain Dhut) is an own-damage claim where the insurer was absolved due to a fake licence, but the Supreme Court expressly limited this to non-third-party claims. It does not apply to the typical third-party claim scenario.

enmity, bias, or mala fides has been brought on record to cast doubt on their depositions.
28. The site plan further fortifies the prosecution case. The deceased was standing towards the
kuccha portion near PW-7's shop, away from the metalled road. The petitioner, while driving a
pick-up vehicle, approached from village Dobhi, failed to negotiate the T-point, and crossed the
entire width of the road before striking the deceased. Such conduct either indicates high speed or
gross lack of control. The doctrine of res ipsa loquitur squarely applies and the very manner of
accident demonstrates negligence on part of the driver. The deceased, who was merely standing off
the road, cannot by any stretch be attributed contributory negligence.
29. In so far as the plea regarding non-establishment of the petitioner's identity is concerned, the
same deserves outright rejection.

on of events is corroborated by the site plan
placed on the record as Ex.PW3/E. The site plan clearly marks point 10 of 32 CRR-2406-2025
(O&M) 'A' as the place where the deceased was struck by the vehicle. Notably, point 'A' is situated on
the side of the road, an area typically used by pedestrians. It is important to highlight that the
accused has not taken any specific defence to the effect that the deceased was crossing the road
recklessly, walking in the middle of the road, or that he had suddenly come in front of the vehicle.
There is no suggestion from the defence that the deceased contributed to the accident in any
manner. On the contrary, it is clearly evident from the site plan and the testimonies on record that
the deceased was walking on the side of the road, in an area normally occupied by pedestrians.
Moreover, the site plan also indicates that the location of the accident was surrounded by several
shops, stalls, and hawkers on both sides of the road, suggesting that it was a congested or densely
populated commercial area. In such surroundings, a higher degree of caution and vigilance is
expected from any person driving a motor vehicle. The legal position is well established that when a
driver is operating a vehicle in a crowded or busy locality, the standard of care required is
considerably higher, and any deviation from that duty amounts to negligence. Driving in a rash and
negligent manner in a busy area enhances culpability. In the present case, both key witnesses the
complainant Satish (PW-6) and Vikas (PW-7) 11 of 32 CRR-2406-2025 (O&M) have consistently
deposed regarding the rash and negligent driving of the accused. Their depositions have remained
unshaken during cross-examination. The accused has not raised any plea of sudden mechanical
failure, poor visibility, or any other mitigating circumstance that could absolve him of criminal
liability. In the absence of any such defence and in light of consistent ocular evidence and
corroborative documentary proof, the prosecution has clearly succeeded in proving the elements of
rashness and negligence on part of the accused.

ct to the medical evidence, it is argued that the deceased remained under continuous
treatment for nearly three weeks and ultimately succumbed to his injuries at MAMCH, Agroha,
Hisar. The contention that his death was the result of repeated changes in medical treatment is,
therefore, unsustainable.

16. It is further contended that the vehicle in question had been released on supurdari to the
petitioner. At no stage did the petitioner disclose the name of any other person who may have been
driving the vehicle at the relevant time. The burden to disclose such a fact squarely lay upon the
registered owner once he raised a plea that he was not the driver. Having failed to discharge this
burden, the petitioner cannot now take advantage of such a plea.
19 of 32 CRR-2406-2025 (O&M)
17. Learned State counsel has thus argued that no amount of monetary compensation can indemnify
the loss of human life, and that the petitioner does not deserve any leniency. The sentence of two
years' rigorous imprisonment as awarded by the learned Judicial Magistrate First Class, Hisar,
cannot be said to be either excessive or harsh. On the contrary, all relevant factors were duly
considered by the trial Court while imposing the sentence.
18. In support of her submissions, reliance has been placed on the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme
Court in State of Punjab v. Balwinder Singh & Others, (2012) 2 SCC 182, wherein it was observed
that deterrence is one of the prime considerations in sentencing for offences relating to rash and
negligent driving, as the alarming rate of motor accidents caused by careless and callous driving
demands stern judicial response.
19. It is, therefore, prayed that the revision petition merits dismissal.
20. I have heard the learned counsel appearing on behalf of the respective parties and have gone
through the documents appended with the present criminal revision petition.
21.

Court is of the considered view that
the prosecution has successfully proved the identity of the accused beyond reasonable
doubt. The accused Sanjay cannot claim any benefit of doubt on this issue. His role as
the driver of the offending vehicle involved in the accident stands clearly established.

15. Now we shall examine the second aspect of the case. In order to establish criminal
liability the "rash or negligent" act by the accused is to be established the prosecution.
The prosecution has to prove that that the negligence or rashness of the accused went
beyond a mere matter of civil liability and he showed such disregard for life and
safety of others as to amount to a crime. In case titled 9 of 32 CRR-2406-2025
(O&M) Mohammed Aynuddin @ Miyam vs State of Andhra 2000(3) RCR (Crl.) 619,
the Apex Court has held that:
"It is wrong proposition that for any motor accident, negligence of driver should be
presumed. To constitute either of the offence under section 279 IPC or section 304-A
IPC, the proof of criminal rashness or criminal negligence is essential. Even in
ordinary parlance 'negligence' connotes want of proper care and 'rashness' conveys
the idea of recklessness or doing of an act without due consideration. The rashness or
negligence must be described as criminal rashness or criminal negligence. "
16. The learned counsel for the appellant/accused has contended that the mere deposition of the
eye-witnesses is insufficient to conclusively establish that the accused was driving the vehicle in a
rash and negligent manner. However, I find no merit in this contention. In the present case, the
prosecution's consistent case is that the deceased Balbir was proceeding from his pushcart (rehri)
towards the khokha of Vikas to attend to the call of nature when he was hit by the vehicle driven by
the accused in a rash and negligent manner. This version of events is corroborated by the site plan
placed on the record as Ex.PW3/E. The site plan clearly marks point 10 of 32 CRR-2406-2025
(O&M) 'A' as the place where the deceased was struck by the vehicle. Notably, point 'A' is situated on
the side of the road, an area typically used by pedestrians.

args.question: What must an owner do to check a driver's licence before employing them, and does failing to check defeat the insurer's defence?

supporting.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
supporting.principle: The owner's duty is to check whether the driver produces a driving licence which on the face of it looks genuine, and to take a test of the driver's competence. The owner is NOT expected to make enquiries with RTOs across the country to verify whether the licence is valid.
supporting.fact_alignment: The owner remained ex parte and adduced no evidence of having checked the licence. The court still held the insurer liable to pay third parties with recovery rights, not that the owner's failure defeated the insurer's defence.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the clearest statement in the corpus of what the owner must do. It quotes Lehru (2003) 3 SCC 338 verbatim: 'When an owner is hiring a driver he will therefore have to check whether the driver has a driving licence. If the driver produces a driving licence which on the face of it looks genuine, the owner is not expected to find out whether the licence has in fact been issued by a competent authority or not.'
supporting.quote: When an owner is hiring a driver he will therefore have to check whether the driver has a driving licence. If the driver produces a driving licence which on the face of it looks genuine, the owner is not expected to find out whether the licence has in fact been issued by a competent authority or not. The owner would then take the test of the driver. If he finds that the driver is competent to drive the vehicle, he will hire the driver.

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: The insurer has a statutory liability to pay third-party compensation even if there is a breach of policy conditions (invalid driving licence), and is entitled to recover from the insured. The owner's failure to check does not defeat the insurer's defence entirely — it triggers pay-and-recover.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver was not competent to drive a transport/commercial vehicle. The court held the insurer liable to pay third parties with recovery rights.
supporting.why_it_matters: Establishes that even where breach is proved, the insurer's remedy is pay-and-recover, not complete absolution, in third-party claims. The owner's failure to check does not let the insurer off the hook to the third party.
supporting.quote: The insurer who is made statutorily liable to pay compensation to third parties on account of the certificate of insurance issued shall be entitled to recover from the insured the amount paid to the third parties, if there was any breach of policy conditions on account of the vehicle being driven without a valid driving licence.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
supporting.principle: Where the driver holds only an LMV licence without the specific authorisation/badge required to drive a transport vehicle, there is a breach of policy conditions. The insurer must pay the third party and recover from the insured owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had an LMV licence but no badge/authorisation to drive a tourist maxi cab (transport vehicle). The insurer proved the breach through the Motor Vehicles Inspector's evidence.
supporting.why_it_matters: Shows the insurer can discharge its burden of proving breach by examining the Motor Vehicles Inspector and adducing licence records. Once breach is proved, the remedy is pay-and-recover, not complete avoidance.
supporting.quote: The absence of any endorsement in the driving licence as to the issuance of authorisation to drive the transport vehicle and non-mention of allotment of badge number clearly shows that the 3rd Respondent was not in possession of a valid driving licence and that he was not duly licensed to drive the transport vehicle and there was violation of Policy conditions.

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Driving without a valid licence constitutes a fundamental and statutory breach of the insurance policy. However, to protect third-party rights, the insurer must pay first and recover from the owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: The owner allowed the driver to drive despite the driver having no driving licence at all. The owner did not produce the driver's licence despite being represented by counsel.
supporting.why_it_matters: Even in the most extreme case — no licence at all — the remedy is pay-and-recover, not complete absolution. The owner's failure to check does not defeat the insurer's defence; it triggers the pay-and-recover mechanism.
supporting.quote: When it is found that offending vehicle was driven by driver who was either holding no licence or a fake licence, then it amounts to violation of terms and conditions of policy and no liability can be fastened upon Insurance Company... But, on the said ground, the petitioner is third party, cannot be made to suffer due to fault of owner when the vehicle is covered with insurance at relevant point of time.

supporting.title: New India Assurance Co., Ltd., vs Yallavva W/O Yamanappa Dharnakeri
supporting.principle: Even if a breach of policy conditions under Section 149(2) is successfully proved, the insurer is bound to satisfy the third-party award and recover from the insured, unless fraud or collusion between the victim and the insured is established.
supporting.fact_alignment: Full Bench decision establishing that pay-and-recover applies to all breaches of policy conditions in third-party claims, regardless of whether the policy is statutory or contractual.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the strongest authority for the proposition that failing to check the licence does NOT defeat the insurer's defence — the insurer still gets pay-and-recover. The only exception is fraud/collusion between victim and insured.
supporting.quote: Even if there is any violation or breach of condition of a policy, the insurer has to discharge the initial burden of proving the grounds taken under Section 149(2) of the Act. In spite of that, the insurer has to indemnify the amount and can recover the same from the insured.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
supporting.principle: Where a special endorsement is required (e.g., for hazardous goods), the owner has a duty under Rule 132(5) of the Central Motor Vehicles Rules to ensure the driver holds the requisite endorsement. Failure constitutes breach entitling the insurer to pay-and-recover.
supporting.fact_alignment: The tanker driver had a valid licence for HGV/HTV but lacked the special endorsement for carrying hazardous goods. The court held the insurer liable to pay and recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Extends the owner's duty beyond just checking for a licence — the owner must also check that the driver has the specific endorsements required for the type of goods being carried. But even here, the remedy is pay-and-recover.
supporting.quote: As per Rule 132 (5) of Central Motor Vehicle Rule, 1989, it is the duty of the owner to ensure that the driver of the goods carriage carrying dangerous or hazardous goods holds a driving license as per the rule 9 of the aforesaid Central Motor Vehicles Rules.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd., vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar W/O Late ...
supporting.principle: When a driving licence is renewed more than 30 days after expiry, it takes effect only from the date of renewal and does not cover the interregnum. The owner who entrusts the vehicle during this period bears responsibility, but the insurer must still pay and recover.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver's licence expired on 30-04-2008, was renewed on 04-07-2008, and the accident occurred on 02-07-2008. The court held the driver did not hold a valid licence on the accident date.
supporting.why_it_matters: Even where the licence had lapsed and the owner entrusted the vehicle to a driver without a current licence, the remedy is pay-and-recover, not complete absolution of the insurer.
supporting.quote: Since it is the statutory right of the third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded either from the owner or the driver, as the vehicle in question is insured, the insurance company shall pay the amount and recover the same from driver or the insured.

supporting.title: National Insurance Company Ltd. Thr. ... vs Smt. Meena And 4 Others
supporting.principle: Even where the driver lacks a valid driving licence, the insurer is liable to pay compensation to third-party claimants and has a right to recover the amount from the insured owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver of the tanker did not have a valid driving licence. The court dismissed the insurer's appeal and upheld the pay-and-recover order.
supporting.why_it_matters: Reinforces the consistent line of authority: the insurer's remedy for licence breach in third-party claims is pay-and-recover, not complete absolution. The court applied S. Iyyapan and Swaran Singh.
supporting.quote: If the driver of the vehicle does not possess valid driving license, insurer is liable to pay compensation to the claimants and further it can recover the amount of compensation from the insured i.e. owner of the vehicle.

adverse.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
adverse.principle: An insurer cannot avoid its statutory liability to pay compensation to third parties merely because the driver of a light motor vehicle did not have a specific endorsement on their licence to drive it as a commercial vehicle.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this to argue that the insurer cannot avoid liability at all — not even pay-and-recover — when the driver held a valid LMV licence but lacked a commercial endorsement. The Supreme Court held the insurer liable without granting recovery rights.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case turned on the specific finding that a Mahindra Maxi Cab is a light motor vehicle and the driver held a valid LMV licence. The Supreme Court held that no separate endorsement was needed to drive it as a commercial vehicle. This is distinguishable where: (a) the vehicle is a different class (e.g., heavy goods vehicle requiring a separate licence class), or (b) the driver had no licence at all, or (c) the licence was fake. The ratio is limited to the LMV/commercial endorsement overlap.
adverse.quote: Merely because the driver did not get any endorsement in the driving licence to drive Mahindra Maxi Cab, which is a light motor vehicle, the High Court has committed grave error of law in holding that the insurer is not liable to pay compensation because the driver was not holding the licence to drive the commercial vehicle.

adverse.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
adverse.principle: The mere non-renewal of an otherwise valid driving licence on the date of accident does not constitute a fundamental breach absolving the insurer of its third-party liability. The insurer is jointly and severally liable without recovery rights.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this to argue that an expired-but-subsequently-renewed licence is not a fundamental breach, and the insurer must pay without recovery rights. This directly undermines the insurer's defence that the owner failed to check licence currency.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case involved licences that had expired but were renewed shortly after the accident. The court emphasised that the drivers had held valid licences, were not disqualified, and the renewal showed they were always entitled to drive. Distinguishable where: (a) the licence was never renewed, (b) the gap between expiry and renewal exceeded 30 days (see doc_003, Parvathi Hebbar), or (c) the driver never held a valid licence for that class of vehicle at all.
adverse.quote: Mere fact that the driver of the offending vehicle had not got his driving licence renewed on the date of the accident and got it renewed subsequently would not amount to breach of condition of the policy as it cannot be said that there was violation of the condition of the exclusion clause.

adverse.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
adverse.principle: Driving without a valid licence is a fundamental and statutory breach. The insurer is not liable to indemnify the owner.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite the portion where the tribunal says 'the insurer is not liable to pay the compensation and he is absolved from its liability' to argue that the insurer should be completely absolved, leaving the claimant to recover only from the owner — which is worse for the claimant, so this is actually a double-edged sword. The claimant would not want this outcome.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: Despite stating that the insurer is 'absolved from its liability', the tribunal ultimately ordered pay-and-recover to protect the third party. The claimant cannot extract the absolving language while ignoring the operative pay-and-recover order. The consistent line of authority (doc_025, doc_033, doc_027) confirms that third-party protection overrides the breach. Moreover, the claimant would not want this outcome — it would leave them recovering only from the owner.
adverse.quote: It is held that the respondent No.2 is not liable to pay the compensation and he is absolved from its liability... But, on the said ground, the petitioner is third party, cannot be made to suffer due to fault of owner when the vehicle is covered with insurance at relevant point of time.

adverse.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
adverse.principle: The Swaran Singh principles regarding third-party risks have no application to own-damage claims. A fake driving licence cannot be cured by subsequent renewal.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this to argue the opposite — that Swaran Singh DOES apply to third-party claims (which is the present context), and therefore the insurer must pay and recover. The case actually supports the insurer on the own-damage vs third-party distinction.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This judgment actually supports the insurer's position on the key point: it confirms that in third-party claims, the insurer must indemnify and recover from the insured. It only limits Swaran Singh for own-damage claims. The claimant will cite it for the proposition that a fake licence cannot be cured, but in third-party claims the insurer still has to pay and recover.
adverse.quote: The decision in Swaran Singh's case has no application to cases other than third party risks... In case of third party risks the insurer has to indemnify the amount and if so advised to recover the same from the insured.

priority_arguments: 1. The owner's duty is limited: the owner need only check that the driver produces a licence that looks genuine on its face and take a test of driving competence. The owner is NOT required to verify with the RTO whether the licence is genuine (doc_027, quoting Lehru).

2. Even if the owner failed to check the licence entirely, the insurer's remedy in third-party claims is pay-and-recover, not complete absolution. The insurer must pay the claimant and then recover from the owner (doc_025, doc_033, doc_035, doc_024, doc_003, doc_006).

3. The burden of proving breach is on the insurer. The insurer must prove not just that the driver lacked a valid licence, but that the owner was guilty of negligence or failed to exercise reasonable care (doc_027, doc_025, citing Swaran Singh).
4. Where the owner remained ex parte or adduced no evidence of having checked the licence, an adverse inference may be drawn, but the remedy remains pay-and-recover, not complete avoidance (doc_027).
5. The only exception where the insurer may be completely absolved is fraud or collusion between the victim and the insured (doc_025), which is extremely rare and fact-specific.
strategy.compensation_range: Not applicable — this is a liability/defence question, not a quantum question.
risks: 1. S.Iyyapan (doc_032) — Supreme Court held that missing commercial endorsement on an LMV licence does not let the insurer off the hook at all (no recovery rights). This is the most dangerous precedent for the insurer. Must be distinguished on vehicle class.

2. K.G. Srinivasamurthy (doc_034) — expired-but-renewed licence held not a fundamental breach; insurer liable without recovery. Must be distinguished where the licence gap exceeds 30 days or was never renewed.
3. The claimant may argue that the insurer must prove 'willful breach' by the owner — mere failure to check may not suffice if the licence looked genuine on its face (doc_027, doc_033).
4. If the insurer cannot prove the licence defect at all (e.g., no evidence from the RTO/MVI), the defence fails entirely and the insurer must pay without any recovery right.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: In third-party claims before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, the insurer should: (a) lead evidence from the Motor Vehicles Inspector/RTO to prove the licence defect; (b) examine the policy to show the relevant condition; (c) argue that breach is proved; but (d) concede that the third party must be paid, and seek a pay-and-recover order against the owner. Do NOT argue for complete absolution in third-party claims — the consistent line of authority rejects this. Reserve the argument for complete absolution only in own-damage claims (doc_031) or where fraud/collusion is proved.

caveats: doc_007 (Harpreet Singh) — concerns dependency/quantum only, no bearing on licence checking or owner's duty.
doc_009 (Kamal) — about contributory negligence of an injured rider driving without a licence; the insurer was held liable. Not about owner's duty to check a driver's licence before employing them.
doc_014 (Shivlal) — gratuitous passenger in goods vehicle; insurer absolved on that ground, not on licence checking.
doc_016 (State of HP) — criminal revision about whether absence of licence constitutes criminal negligence. Holds it does not. Not about owner's civil duty to check licence.
doc_017 (Sanjay) — criminal case about rash driving. No bearing on owner's duty to verify licence.
doc_029 (Minor Mahesh) — gratuitous passengers in goods vehicle/tractor; insurer absolved on that ground, not on licence checking.
doc_038 (Crown Consultants) — insurance claim repudiation for late filing. No connection to licence verification.

payload.holding: The Tribunal erred in passing an order of 'pay and recover' against the insurance company when passengers travelling in a private vehicle for hire or reward are not third parties and their risk is not covered under the Act policy, and therefore the insurer is completely exonerated.
payload.ratio: Where a passenger is travelling in a private vehicle for hire or reward in breach of policy conditions, such a passenger is not a 'third party' under the Act policy, and the Tribunal or Court cannot invoke 'pay and recover' to compel the insurer to satisfy the award and recover from the owner.

priority_arguments: 1. The owner's duty is limited: the owner need only check that the driver produces a licence that looks genuine on its face and take a test of driving competence. The owner is NOT required to verify with the RTO whether the licence is genuine (doc_027, quoting Lehru).

2. Even if the owner failed to check the licence entirely, the insurer's remedy in third-party claims is pay-and-recover, not complete absolution. The insurer must pay the claimant and then recover from the owner (doc_025, doc_033, doc_035, doc_024, doc_003, doc_006).

3. The burden of proving breach is on the insurer. The insurer must prove not just that the driver lacked a valid licence, but that the owner was guilty of negligence or failed to exercise reasonable care (doc_027, doc_025, citing Swaran Singh).
4. Where the owner remained ex parte or adduced no evidence of having checked the licence, an adverse inference may be drawn, but the remedy remains pay-and-recover, not complete avoidance (doc_027).
5. The only exception where the insurer may be completely absolved is fraud or collusion between the victim and the insured (doc_025), which is extremely rare and fact-specific.

risks: 1. S.Iyyapan (doc_032) — Supreme Court held that missing commercial endorsement on an LMV licence does not let the insurer off the hook at all (no recovery rights). This is the most dangerous precedent for the insurer. Must be distinguished on vehicle class.

2. K.G. Srinivasamurthy (doc_034) — expired-but-renewed licence held not a fundamental breach; insurer liable without recovery. Must be distinguished where the licence gap exceeds 30 days or was never renewed.
3. The claimant may argue that the insurer must prove 'willful breach' by the owner — mere failure to check may not suffice if the licence looked genuine on its face (doc_027, doc_033).
4. If the insurer cannot prove the licence defect at all (e.g., no evidence from the RTO/MVI), the defence fails entirely and the insurer must pay without any recovery right.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: In third-party claims before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, the insurer should: (a) lead evidence from the Motor Vehicles Inspector/RTO to prove the licence defect; (b) examine the policy to show the relevant condition; (c) argue that breach is proved; but (d) concede that the third party must be paid, and seek a pay-and-recover order against the owner. Do NOT argue for complete absolution in third-party claims — the consistent line of authority rejects this. Reserve the argument for complete absolution only in own-damage claims (doc_031) or where fraud/collusion is proved.

caveats: doc_002 (Liyakat Ali) — outcome favours insurer but on an entirely different ground: tractor used for non-agricultural purposes in breach of policy. No bearing on licence checking or owner's duty to verify a driver's licence.
doc_007 (Harpreet Singh) — concerns dependency/quantum only, no bearing on licence checking or owner's duty.
doc_009 (Kamal) — about contributory negligence of an injured rider driving without a licence; the insurer was held liable. Not about owner's duty to check a driver's licence before employing them.
doc_014 (Shivlal) — gratuitous passenger in goods vehicle; insurer absolved on that ground, not on licence checking.
doc_016 (State of HP) — criminal revision about whether absence of licence constitutes criminal negligence. Holds it does not. Not about owner's civil duty to check licence.
doc_017 (Sanjay) — criminal case about rash driving. No bearing on owner's duty to verify licence.

doc_028 (Sukumarbai) — outcome favours insurer but on an entirely different ground: passengers in a private vehicle for hire are not third parties. No bearing on licence checking or owner's duty to verify a driver's licence.
doc_029 (Minor Mahesh) — gratuitous passengers in goods vehicle/tractor; insurer absolved on that ground, not on licence checking.
doc_038 (Crown Consultants) — insurance claim repudiation for late filing. No connection to licence verification.

risks: 1. S.Iyyapan (doc_032) — Supreme Court held that missing commercial endorsement on an LMV licence does not let the insurer off the hook at all (no recovery rights). This is the most dangerous precedent for the insurer. Must be distinguished on vehicle class.

2. K.G. Srinivasamurthy (doc_034) — expired-but-renewed licence held not a fundamental breach; insurer liable without recovery. Must be distinguished where the licence gap exceeds 30 days or was never renewed.
3. The claimant may argue that the insurer must prove 'willful breach' by the owner — mere failure to check may not suffice if the licence looked genuine on its face (doc_027, doc_033).
4. If the insurer cannot prove the licence defect at all (e.g., no evidence from the RTO/MVI), the defence fails entirely and the insurer must pay without any recovery right.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: In third-party claims before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, the insurer should: (a) lead evidence from the Motor Vehicles Inspector/RTO to prove the licence defect; (b) examine the policy to show the relevant condition; (c) argue that breach is proved; but (d) concede that the third party must be paid, and seek a pay-and-recover order against the owner. Do NOT argue for complete absolution in third-party claims — the consistent line of authority rejects this. Reserve the argument for complete absolution only in own-damage claims (doc_031) or where fraud/collusion is proved.

caveats: doc_002 (Liyakat Ali) — outcome favours insurer but on an entirely different ground: tractor used for non-agricultural purposes in breach of policy. No bearing on licence checking or owner's duty to verify a driver's licence.
doc_007 (Harpreet Singh) — concerns dependency/quantum only, no bearing on licence checking or owner's duty.
doc_009 (Kamal) — about contributory negligence of an injured rider driving without a licence; the insurer was held liable. Not about owner's duty to check a driver's licence before employing them.
doc_014 (Shivlal) — gratuitous passenger in goods vehicle; insurer absolved on that ground, not on licence checking.
doc_016 (State of HP) — criminal revision about whether absence of licence constitutes criminal negligence. Holds it does not. Not about owner's civil duty to check licence.
doc_017 (Sanjay) — criminal case about rash driving. No bearing on owner's duty to verify licence.

doc_028 (Sukumarbai) — outcome favours insurer but on an entirely different ground: passengers in a private vehicle for hire are not third parties. No bearing on licence checking or owner's duty to verify a driver's licence.
doc_029 (Minor Mahesh) — gratuitous passengers in goods vehicle/tractor; insurer absolved on that ground, not on licence checking.
doc_038 (Crown Consultants) — insurance claim repudiation for late filing. No connection to licence verification.
